items.title: Can machines think?
items.intro: Documented milestones in how the question has been posed. These are scholarly sources; the list is a selection, not a complete history, and it does not yet include earlier philosophical discussion because no verified sources for that have been reviewed.

entries.title: Turing proposes the imitation game
entries.text: Opens with 'Can machines think?' and replaces it with a behavioral game played through typed questions and answers.

entries.title: The Dartmouth proposal
entries.text: Proposes a two-month, ten-person study in summer 1956, resting on the premise that any feature of intelligence could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.

entries.title: Searle's 'Minds, brains, and programs'
entries.text: Argues that running a program is never by itself sufficient for intentionality, and that strong AI cannot succeed.

entries.title: A language model evaluated without weight updates
entries.text: Brown et al. report GPT-3's task performance and raise methodological concerns tied to web-scraped training data. The abstract makes no claim about understanding.

entries.title: An indicator approach to AI consciousness
entries.text: Butlin et al. propose assessing AI systems against indicator properties derived from scientific theories and conclude that no current AI systems appear to be conscious.

items.title: How can consciousness be studied?
items.intro: A selection of documented milestones in how scholars have framed and tested the problem. It is not a complete history.

entries.title: Nagel: 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?'
entries.text: States that an organism has conscious states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism, and argues reductive analyses leave out subjective character.

entries.title: Chalmers: 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness'
entries.text: Separates the hard core of the problem from its tractable parts and argues for a nonreductive approach.

entries.title: Seth and Bayne review four theoretical approaches
entries.text: Compares higher-order, global workspace, re-entry and predictive processing, and integrated information theories, and considers how they might be distinguished empirically.

entries.title: A preregistered adversarial collaboration protocol (GNWT vs IIT)
entries.text: States contrasting predictions about where and when the neural correlates of visual consciousness occur.

entries.title: Results of an adversarial collaboration reported
entries.text: The Cogitate authors report results that partly align with and substantially challenge key claims of both GNWT and IIT.
